messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark, a 58-year-old dentist in a long-term relationship, still flinched every time a patient’s shadow fell across the operatory doorway—a reflex that had begun three years earlier, after a traffic stop turned into what he could only describe as a beating. He had been driving home from a late appointment when two officers mistook his sedan for a stolen vehicle, pulled him out, and spent several minutes on his back and ribs while he pleaded. The memory returned not as a coherent story but as pieces that belonged to someone else: the metallic crunch of a boot against his spine, the scrape of asphalt across his cheek, the officer’s voice ordering him to stay down. He knew it had happened to him, yet the scenes felt like a film he had stumbled into by mistake. That sense of dislocation was the only way his mind seemed able to hold what his body had endured.

Over the following months, Mark became convinced that some flaw in him had drawn the violence. He replayed the moment the patrol car’s lights came on and asked himself what he could have said, how he could have looked, to signal *different*—as if his own face or posture had been an invitation. This belief that his intrinsic fault was to blame made the memories feel even more alien; they belonged to a version of himself who had been weak or wrong, a person he no longer recognized. When the auditory flashbacks came—a sharp command, a crack of radio static—his ribs would ache as if freshly struck, and he would wonder whether the man in those sounds was even him.

To keep the memories at bay, Mark began steering his life into a narrow channel. He avoided anything that might stir emotion, positive or negative, because feeling anything seemed to crack the seal on the pain recall. He cancelled a dinner with old friends because the restaurant would be crowded and unpredictable. At his dental practice, he outfitted the waiting room with partitions so he could not see who was approaching the front desk, and he arranged his own operatory chair so his back faced a solid wall. He checked every new patient’s name, then scanned the hallway before leaving a room. Still, the threat of strangers felt constant: a man walking too close on the sidewalk, a delivery driver who lingered at the door—each one triggered a spike of auditory recall, the officer’s voice overlapping with the present moment, and a fresh wave of pain in his lower back.

That sense of threat also worsened his sleep. He lay awake listening for footsteps in the hall, his body braced, and when he finally drifted off, the dream version of the stop always ended with a blow he could not avoid. Waking from these nightmares, he would lie rigid and replay the injustice: no charges were filed, no apology came, the officers’ names were never released. That feeling of being crushed by an unfair system reinforced his belief that his life had been destroyed—not just physically but morally, chronologically. Every avoidance, every checking of the room, every refusal to let a stranger stand behind him at a checkout line only confirmed that he was now a person who had to live this way.

The patterns tightened into a loop he could not see. Because he avoided all stress, he never went to the small park where he used to walk; because he never walked there, he never gave himself the chance to learn that strangers on a path were not officers with badges. Because he checked his surroundings compulsively, he stayed hypervigilant, and hypervigilance kept the auditory recall present. The alien quality of the memory—the sense that the whole event had happened to a different man—meant he could not integrate it into his story, so it stayed raw and easily triggered. And each triggered memory reaffirmed that he was fundamentally marked, that the injustice was permanent, that his life was over.

What finally brought Mark to a therapist was his partner’s quiet observation that he had not touched her in months—not out of anger but because he had shut down all feeling, even affection. He came not hoping to erase the memory, but terrified that he might never again feel like the person he had been before the lights came on in his rearview mirror.
